summary: Give the Transferrin saturation calculator the serum iron concentration (Fe) and the transferrin saturation (TSAT) and it returns total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Transferrin saturation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Transferrin saturation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the serum iron concentration (Fe) (First method), the transferrin saturation (TSAT) (First method), the serum iron concentration (Fe) (Second method) and the transferrin saturation (TSAT) (Second method).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Transferrin saturation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)=serum iron concentration (Fe) ÷ transferrin saturation (TSAT)
Serum transferrin concentration (TF)=(709 ÷ 10) × serum iron concentration (Fe) ÷ transferrin saturation (TSAT)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Serum iron concentration (Fe) = 10 µg/dL and Transferrin saturation (TSAT) = 10 %. Working through the relationship above gives Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) = 100 µg/dL.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) = 100 µg/dL should be roughly the size you expected from Serum iron concentration (Fe) = 10 µg/dL and Transferrin saturation (TSAT) = 10 %.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in micrograms per deciliter, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • Shown in milligrams per deciliter, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Density, opening in micrograms per deciliter
  • Density, opening in micrograms per deciliter
  • %, opening in percent
  • Density, opening in micrograms per deciliter
  • Density, opening in milligrams per deciliter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Transferrin saturation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the serum iron concentration (Fe) and the transferrin saturation (TSAT) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Transferrin saturation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), derived from the serum iron concentration (Fe) and the transferrin saturation (TSAT). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Transferrin saturation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the serum iron concentration (Fe) and the transferrin saturation (TSAT), which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter serum iron concentration (Fe) (First method) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Serum iron concentration (Fe) (First method) opens in micrograms per deciliter and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) = 100 µg/dL. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Transferrin saturation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
